problem: Source "between hoar and knotty shafts" (grey/white, knotted trunks); modern invents "moss-grown".
new_text: I reached this house just before dark on an evening marked by grey skies, a cold wind, and steady, penetrating rain. The last mile I walked, having dismissed the carriage and driver with the double payment I'd promised. Even when I was very close to the manor, I could see nothing of it—so thick and dark were the trees of the gloomy wood around it. Iron gates between granite pillars showed me where to enter. Passing through them, I found myself at once in the twilight of close-ranked trees. A grass-grown track led down the forest aisle between grey, knotted trunks and under arching branches. I followed it, expecting soon to reach the house, but it stretched on and on, winding farther and farther, with no sign of any dwelling or grounds.

problem: "The darkness of natural as well as of sylvan dusk" (nightfall plus the forest's shade) is rendered as "The darkness of nature and forest", which is hard to parse.
new_text: I thought I had taken a wrong turn and lost my way. The darkness of nightfall, as well as the dusk of the forest, gathered around me. I looked for another path. There was none—only interwoven branches, thick trunks, and dense summer foliage. Not an opening anywhere.

problem: Source names "the host of the Rochester Arms"; modern reduces it to an anonymous "the innkeeper", losing the link to the earlier chapter.
new_text: I kept going. At last the trees thinned a little. Soon I made out a railing, then the house—barely distinguishable from the trees in the dim light, so damp and green were its decaying walls. I entered through a door fastened only with a latch and stood in an enclosed yard from which the wood curved away in a half circle. There were no flowers, no garden beds—only a broad gravel walk circling a patch of grass, set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front. The windows were latticed and narrow. The front door was narrow too—one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the landlord of the Rochester Arms had said, "quite a desolate spot." It was as still as a church on a weekday—the only sound anywhere around was the rain pattering on the forest leaves.

problem: Source "nor were his features altered or sunk" (unchanged, not hollowed); modern invents "still sharp and firm".
new_text: His form was the same strong, powerful build as ever. His bearing was still upright. His hair was still raven-black. Nor were his features altered or sunken—not in one year's time could any sorrow have worn down his athletic strength or blighted his prime. But in his face I saw a change—a look of desperate brooding that reminded me of some wronged and chained wild animal or bird, dangerous to approach in its sullen misery. A caged eagle, its gold-ringed eyes put out by cruelty, might have looked as that blind Samson looked.

problem: Source simply has John speak ("he said") and ask "had you not better go in?"; modern invents "said a voice. It was John." (John was already introduced in 37.10) and turns the deferential question into a command.
new_text: "Will you take my arm, sir?" he said. "There's a heavy shower coming on. Hadn't you better go in?"

problem: Source: "re-entering it, closed the door" (Jane sees it); modern invents "I heard him close the door".
new_text: John withdrew without noticing me. Mr. Rochester tried again to walk about—in vain. Everything was too uncertain. He groped his way back to the house, went in again, and closed the door.

problem: Source image "my heart struck my ribs loud and fast" flattened to "My heart pounded."
new_text: I took it from her hand. She pointed me toward the parlour door. The tray shook as I held it. The water sloshed from the glass. My heart beat loud and fast against my ribs. Mary opened the door for me and shut it behind me.

problem: Dropped details: Pilot lay "removed out of the way", and jumped up "with a yelp and a whine".
new_text: The parlour looked grim. A neglected handful of fire burned low in the grate. Leaning over it, with his head supported against the tall, old-fashioned mantelpiece, stood the blind tenant of the room. His old dog, Pilot, lay on one side, out of the way, curled up as if afraid of being accidentally stepped on. Pilot pricked his ears when I came in. Then he jumped up with a yelp and a whine, and bounded toward me. He almost knocked the tray from my hands. I set it on the table, then patted him and said softly, "Lie down!" Mr. Rochester turned mechanically to see what the commotion was, but since he saw nothing, he turned back and sighed.

problem: Source "my life dark, lonely, hopeless" drops "hopeless".
new_text: "Never will, says the vision? But I always woke and found it an empty mockery. And I was desolate and abandoned—my life dark, lonely, hopeless—my soul thirsting and forbidden to drink—my heart starved and never fed. Gentle, soft dream, nestled in my arms now, you will fly too, as all your sisters fled before you—but kiss me before you go. Embrace me, Jane."

problem: Source "dead in some ditch under some stream" drops "under some stream"; "pining outcast" (wasting with longing) becomes "starving outcast".
new_text: "And you do not lie dead in some ditch under some stream? And you are not a pining outcast among strangers?"

problem: Source "a blind lameter like me" (a blind, lame man); modern drops the lameness: "a blind man like me".
new_text: "But as you're rich, Jane, you must now have friends who will look after you and not let you devote yourself to a blind, lame man like me?"

new_text: "No, my fairy. But I am only too thankful to hear and feel you."

new_text: "Yet I have been with good people—far better than you. A hundred times better. People with ideas and views you never entertained in your life. Much more refined and exalted."

problem: Source "You mocking changeling—fairy-born and human-bred!"; "changeling" (the fairy-child image the rest of the line depends on) is flattened to "creature".
new_text: "You mocking changeling—fairy-born and human-raised! You make me feel as I haven't felt in twelve months. If Saul could have had you for his David, the evil spirit would have been exorcised without the need for a harp."

problem: Rochester's anxious question "Was it dry?" is dropped.
new_text: Very early the next morning I heard him up and moving about, wandering from one room to another. As soon as Mary came down, I heard the question: "Is Miss Eyre here?" Then: "Which room did you put her in? Was it dry? Is she up? Go and ask if she wants anything. And when she'll come down."

problem: Source quotes French "'Jeune encore,' as the French say"; modern drops the French and the attribution. Guidance: keep French where the source gives it.
new_text: "'Jeune encore,' as the French say—still young. Is he a short, dull, plain man? The kind whose goodness lies more in the absence of vice than in any real strength of character?"

new_text: "The picture you've just painted suggests a rather overwhelming contrast. Your words have sketched very prettily a graceful Apollo—he is present to your imagination: tall, fair, blue-eyed, with a Grecian profile. Your eyes rest on a Vulcan—a real blacksmith, brown, broad-shouldered, and blind and lame into the bargain."

problem: Jane's teasing hedge "rather like Vulcan" becomes the flat "do resemble".
new_text: "I never thought of it before, but you certainly are rather like Vulcan, sir."

problem: Source "He wanted you to marry him?" is a probing question (Jane answers with a correction, "He asked me"); modern makes it an assertion.
new_text: "Ah! Now we reach the heart of the matter. He wanted you to marry him?"

problem: "I'll not leave you of my own accord" rendered "I won't leave on my own", which can be heard as "leave alone/unaccompanied".
new_text: "Shake me off, then, sir—push me away. I won't leave you of my own accord."

problem: Biblical "become one flesh" flattened to "be joined"; voice guidance asks to keep biblical language.
new_text: "We must become one flesh without delay, Jane. There's only the license to get—then we marry."

problem: "keep it henceforward" (for good) loses "henceforward".
new_text: "Fasten it to your belt, Janet, and keep it from now on. I have no use for it."

problem: Rochester's speech continues into 37.250; the source paragraph has no closing quotation mark (as in 37.248 and 37.254), but modern closes the quote after "Jane."
new_text: "Some days ago—four days, to be exact—last Monday night, a strange mood came over me. Grief replaced frenzy. Sorrow replaced bitterness. I had long been convinced that since I couldn't find you anywhere, you must be dead. Late that night—perhaps between eleven and midnight—before going to my miserable bed, I begged God, if it pleased Him, to take me soon from this life and admit me to the next world, where there was still hope of reunion with Jane.

problem: Dropped "afflicted" from "desolate, afflicted, tormented"; "bliss and peace" weakened to "peace and happiness"; biblical "the alpha and omega of my heart's wishes" flattened to "the sum of my heart's whole desire".
new_text: "I was in my room, sitting by the open window. The mild night air soothed me. I could see no stars—only by a faint, luminous haze did I know the moon was out. I longed for you, Janet! Oh, I longed for you with soul and flesh! I asked God, in anguish and humility, whether I had not been desolate, afflicted, and tormented long enough. Whether I might not soon taste bliss and peace again. I admitted I deserved everything I'd endured—but I pleaded that I could scarcely bear any more. And the alpha and omega of my heart's wishes broke involuntarily from my lips in the words: 'Jane! Jane! Jane!'"

problem: Source ends with the Luke 2:19 allusion "I kept these things then, and pondered them in my heart"; modern drops "pondered".
new_text: Reader, it was on Monday night—near midnight—that I too had received the mysterious call. Those were the very words with which I had answered it. I listened to Mr. Rochester's account but said nothing in return. The coincidence struck me as too strange and awe-inspiring to discuss. If I told anything, my story would inevitably make a deep impression on his mind—and that mind, already too prone to dark thoughts from suffering, did not need the added weight of supernatural mystery. I kept these things, then, and pondered them in my heart.

problem: Source "melt to silence and annihilation" drops "annihilation".
new_text: "You can't wonder, then," my master continued, "that when you appeared before me so unexpectedly last night, I had difficulty believing you were anything more than a voice and a vision—something that would dissolve into silence and nothingness, as the midnight whisper and mountain echo had dissolved before. Now, I thank God! I know otherwise. Yes, I thank God!"

problem: Source: John "had known his master when he was the cadet of the house" (the younger son, not heir, which matters to Rochester's backstory); modern changes it to "since boyhood".
new_text: "I told Mary how it would be," he said. "I knew what Mr. Edward"—John was an old servant who had known his master when he was the younger son of the house, so he often used his first name—"I knew what Mr. Edward would do. And I was certain he wouldn't wait long either. And he's done right, in my opinion. I wish you joy, Miss!" And he politely touched his forehead.

problem: Dialect "she's noan faâl" means "she's not foul" (not ugly), continuing the thought about looks ("If she ben't one o' th' handsomest"); modern mistranslates it as "she's no fool".
new_text: "She'll likely do better for him than any of the grand ladies would have." And again: "If she's not one of the handsomest, she's not ugly, and she's very good-natured. And in his eyes she's beautiful—anyone can see that."

problem: Source: the boy inherited eyes "large, brilliant, and black" (Rochester's characteristic black eyes); modern softens to "dark".
new_text: He and I went to London. He consulted an eminent eye specialist and eventually recovered the sight of that one eye. He cannot see very clearly now. He cannot read or write much. But he can find his way without being led by the hand. The sky is no longer a blank to him—the earth no longer a void. When his firstborn was placed in his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his own eyes, as they once were—large, brilliant, and black. On that occasion, he acknowledged once more, with a full heart, that God had tempered judgment with mercy.

problem: Source "alternately, once every year, they come to see us, and we go to see them" (visits alternate each year) loses "alternately"; "from his attainments and principles, worthy of the connection" becomes a vague "in every respect".
new_text: My Edward and I are happy. And the more so because those we love most are happy too. Diana and Mary Rivers are both married. Once every year, by turns, they come to see us or we go to see them. Diana's husband is a captain in the navy—a brave officer and a good man. Mary's is a clergyman, a college friend of her brother's, and, in his learning and principles, worthy of the connection. Both Captain Fitzjames and Mr. Wharton love their wives and are loved by them.
